chapters.title: Chapter 4: Paying Tax Through the Year

lessons.title: Advance Tax: Instalments, Due Dates and the Interest for Missing Them

body.text: India does not wait until your year ends to collect tax. It expects you to estimate this year's profit while you are still earning it, and to pay in four instalments as you go. Miss them and the interest is charged automatically, without a notice, an argument or a way to appeal.

children.text: Advance tax is the most avoidable cost in this entire course. Nobody disputes the rate, nobody disallows anything, and no assessing officer is involved. A company simply pays later than the law wanted, and the system adds 1% a month for the privilege. Every rupee of it comes out of profit, and none of it is deductible.
Who Pays, and How Much by When

Section 404 [old 208] sets the entry point: advance tax is payable once your estimated tax for the year, after reducing TDS and TCS credits, is ₹10,000 or more. That threshold catches almost every profitable business in the country. Section 405 [old 209] then tells you to estimate current income yourself, apply this year's rates, and subtract the tax others will deduct at source on your behalf.

cells: Estimated from barely two months of actual trading
Half-year numbers are in, so re-estimate rather than repeat June's guess
Nine months of data, the most reliable estimate of the year
Trues up the whole year, two weeks before it ends
Tax paid by this date still counts as advance tax for the year

body.text: Businesses taxed presumptively under section 58 [old 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE] escape the four-instalment schedule entirely and pay their whole advance tax in one go by 15 March. That simplicity is one of the quieter attractions of the presumptive scheme for small proprietors and firms.

children.text: Two Different Interests, Two Different Mistakes

body.title: Section 425 and section 424 punish different failures

columns.label: Section 425 [old 234C]: paying late within the year
points: Triggered when a cumulative instalment target is missed
3% on the shortfall for each of the first three instalments, being 1% a month for three months
1% on the shortfall for the 15 March instalment
Charged even if you pay everything by 31 March

columns.label: Section 424 [old 234B]: not paying enough at all
points: Triggered when advance tax paid is less than 90% of assessed tax
1% per month, running from the start of the next tax year until the tax is paid
Runs on the whole shortfall, month after month, until settled
This is the one that compounds into real money

body.caption: Part of a month counts as a whole month, in both sections

body.title: Worked example: the company that paid nothing until October

children.text: A company's tax for the year comes to ₹40,00,000, with no TDS credits. It pays nothing during the year and settles the full amount in October, when it files its return. Two separate interest charges apply.

Then section 424 [old 234B] applies separately, because the company paid less than 90% of its assessed tax during the year. Interest runs at 1% a month on ₹40,00,000 from the start of the next tax year until it pays in October, which is seven months, or ₹2,80,000.
Total interest is ₹4,82,000 on a ₹40,00,000 liability. That is more than 12% of the tax, paid for nothing but timing, and none of it is deductible when computing next year's income.

body.title: Try It: One Missed Instalment
body.prompt: A company estimates its tax for the year at ₹60,00,000. It pays ₹9,00,000 by 15 June and ₹18,00,000 more by 15 September, both on time, but pays nothing further by 15 December. What interest arises under section 425 [old 234C] for the December instalment alone? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: By 15 December the cumulative requirement is 75% of ₹60,00,000, which is ₹45,00,000. The company has paid ₹27,00,000, so the shortfall is ₹18,00,000. At 3% for that instalment, interest is ₹54,000. Note that the June and September payments of 15% and 45% were exactly on target, which is why no interest arises for those two.

children.text: The Relief for Income You Could Not Have Predicted

The law accepts that some income cannot be estimated in June. Where a shortfall arises because of capital gains or dividend income that had not yet arisen, no interest is charged for the earlier instalments, provided the tax on it is paid in the instalment following the event, or by 31 March. A company that sells land in February is not punished for failing to foresee it in June.

body.text: The relief is narrow. It covers unpredictable one-off income, not an ordinary trading year that turned out better than expected. If your regular business simply grew faster than you estimated in June, the deferment interest applies in full. The fix is not a legal argument, it is re-estimating at each instalment instead of dividing last year's number by four.

body.title: Quick Check: The 15 September Target
body.question: A company estimates its tax for the year at ₹1,00,00,000 and has no TDS credits. How much must it have paid cumulatively by 15 September to avoid interest under section 425 [old 234C]?
body.explanation: The September target is 45% cumulative, so ₹45,00,000, including whatever was paid in June. The schedule is cumulative rather than four equal quarters, which catches people out: by December you must be at 75%, not at three quarters of the way through equal payments of 25% each.

events.title: First instalment, 15%
events.description: Base it on a real forecast, not on last year divided by four. Reduce it by TDS others will deduct on your receipts.

events.title: Second instalment, 45% cumulative
events.description: Re-estimate with half-year actuals. Any June under-estimate can still be corrected here with only the June shortfall carrying interest.

events.title: Third instalment, 75% cumulative
events.description: Your most accurate estimate of the year. Most well-run finance teams treat this as the real forecast checkpoint.

events.title: Fourth instalment, 100%
events.description: True up fully. Paying at least 90% of final tax by 31 March also keeps section 424 [old 234B] away.

events.description: Any remaining tax paid now is self-assessment tax, and section 424 interest has been running on it since the year began.

body.title: Scenario: The Seasonal Business
body.scenario: A Jaipur company sells decorative lighting. Roughly 60% of its annual profit is earned between September and November, around the festive season, and the rest is spread thinly across the year. Its accountant pays advance tax by dividing last year's tax into four equal parts. This year, sales were far stronger than last year, and the company also sold a surplus warehouse in February at a large gain.
body.prompt: Where will interest arise, and how should the company change its approach?
body.modelAnswer: Two separate problems sit in here. The seasonal profit is not one of them in the way the accountant thinks: the instalment schedule is cumulative and back-loaded, at 15%, 45%, 75% and 100%, which already suits a business earning most of its profit in the second half. The real problem is the method. Paying last year's tax in four equal parts means paying 25% by June when only 15% was due, which wastes cash, and then falling short later in a year when profit has grown. Because the growth came from ordinary trading rather than an unforeseeable event, no relief applies, and interest under section 425 [old 234C] will run at 3% on each shortfall, with section 424 [old 234B] at 1% a month on top if the total paid falls below 90% of assessed tax. The warehouse sale is different. Capital gains arising in February could not have been estimated in June, so the relief applies as long as the tax on that gain is paid in the instalment that follows the sale, which here means by 15 March. The fix is procedural, not clever: prepare a fresh profit estimate before each of the four dates, using actual figures to date plus a realistic forecast for the rest of the year, and reduce it by TDS already deducted on the company's receipts. A half-day of work before each instalment saves the entire interest cost.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The 90% Test
body.textWithBlank: Interest under section 424 [old 234B] applies when advance tax paid during the year is less than ___ percent of the assessed tax.
body.explanation: Ninety percent. Clearing that bar by 31 March keeps section 424 away entirely, even if you were late with individual instalments and still owe section 425 interest. It is the single most useful number in this lesson, because section 424 is the charge that keeps running month after month until the tax is finally paid.

body.label: Interest is not a penalty you can argue about
body.context: Sections 424 and 425 operate by arithmetic. There is no discretion to waive them in the ordinary course, no notice required, and the interest cannot be claimed as a business expense.

body.title: A Quarterly Routine That Costs Nothing
steps: Ten days before each due date, prepare a fresh full-year profit estimate from actuals plus forecast
Convert it to tax at your regime's effective rate, including surcharge and cess, not the base rate
Subtract TDS and TCS already deducted on your receipts, and credits shown against your PAN
Compare with the cumulative target of 15%, 45%, 75% or 100% and pay the difference
Pay through the e-Pay Tax facility on the income tax portal, selecting the correct tax year and the advance tax head
Save the challan and reconcile it against your tax credit statement before filing
Flag any large one-off gain immediately, since its tax is due in the instalment following the event

cards.definition: Advance tax applies once estimated tax for the year, after TDS and TCS, is ₹10,000 or more.
How advance tax is computed: estimate current income, apply the year's rates, reduce by tax deductible at source.
The instalment schedule: 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% cumulative by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.
Interest for deferring instalments: 3% on the shortfall for each of the first three, and 1% for the fourth.
Interest at 1% a month where advance tax paid is under 90% of assessed tax, running until the tax is paid.
Interest at 1% a month on unpaid tax when the return itself is filed after the due date.
Tax paid after the year ends, at the time of filing, on which section 424 interest has usually already accrued.

points: Advance tax applies once estimated tax after TDS reaches ₹10,000 under section 404 [old 208], which covers nearly every profitable business
Instalments are cumulative at 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March, under section 408 [old 211]
Section 425 [old 234C] charges 3% on each of the first three shortfalls and 1% on the fourth
Section 424 [old 234B] charges 1% a month whenever advance tax paid is below 90% of assessed tax, and keeps running until you pay
Unforeseeable capital gains and dividend income get relief if taxed in the following instalment or by 31 March, but ordinary business growth does not
Presumptive taxpayers under section 58 pay the whole amount in one instalment by 15 March
None of this interest is deductible, and all of it is avoidable by re-estimating four times a year

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Interest computations depend on exact dates and on the final assessed figures, and due dates can be extended by the CBDT. Confirm your own position with a qualified chartered accountant.
